title: My workflow for creating a trailer video over a weekend
author: nsjames1
selftext:
Been working on a multiplayer 10v10 PvP mobile game, and decided to create a trailer for it using AI on Friday, and did the video over the weekend. 

Just wanted to go over my journey doing it in case it can help anyone here. 



For context: I’m a dev with 20 years exp (gamedev included), as well as a long history with 3d modeling and video production (also professionally). 



I started with the idea, a solo assault trying to capture a point while his team is busy messing around elsewhere instead of trying to win. 



For all the steps below, I used MCPs with claude code. 

I was on the way to pick up my kids from school, and just talking to myself, miming out the characters and the situations they’d be in. I ended up with what I thought was a pretty funny script, and later that night I went back and forth with Claude ironing out the timing and scenes. Turned that into a markdown file.



Then, I had Claude using elevenlabs create voices for the two main characters:

1. The assault - Brutish, big, a little dumb, frustrated
2. The robotics engineer - Annoyed, busy, just wants to finish what he’s doing, doesn’t care about the assault or the win



I generated about 10 voices for each, and then chose one for each and saved those voices as characters on 11labs. Then I regenerated the full audio stems so the emotions/energy/vibe of each character could feed off of the other character. 



Then I had Claude/11labs generate some general sound fx to put underneath so I could feel it out and create a full track of all the audio. After that, I had Claude spawn a bunch of codex agents to generate variations of storyboards which split the video into cinematic shots and gameplay shots (I knew I wanted to blend them). 



It got annoying to go back and forth between the images on disk, so I had Claude build an HTML page to serve as a video editor (looks like adobe premiere/davinci resolve/etc) and slice out the storyboard panels that I liked overlaid on the audio track so that I could keep track. 



My game already has fully rigged 3d models, so I just used those (albeit you can see some artifacts from them never being intended for 1920x1080 close ups, but… it’s got that certain old-tf2-video charm to it imo) and told Claude to get to work going through all the scenes and generating them. It ended up creating a standalone unity3d project to render the videos along with Blender using the MCP, to create a rough pass of the scenes (it started with about 6 of the 18 scenes). First cut… wasn’t great :)



I was cleaning the garage and taking down the halloween decorations so I just plopped my laptop in the garage and came back to it every 10 or so minutes, looked at what it did, prompted for changes, and iterated until I got to scene compositions and timings that I was happy with. 



For the music and sound effects, I ended up going with a blend of both being generated with 11labs or found on envato elements, or found on elements and fed into 11labs as source to change them (music was done that way, since I wanted happy in the beginning, but suspenseful towards the end).



There are a few scenes with anime/comic style effects. For those I just took a screenshot of the frame as it was, pasted it into chatgpt and told it to add anime/comic style effects (with a better prompt of course lol). Then I took those back to Claude, and iterated with it until I got something I was happy with (it desperately tried to use codex to generate animations via multiple images, and that was almost always the worst outcome, so I had it use real shaders and materials / vfx instead)



I’d say I spent around 5-6 hours a day over the weekend prompting away, and honestly, I’m pretty impressed with the outcome, and more importantly the speed. I \_could\_ have done a better job manually (at least in some parts, like animations), but it would have taken me significantly longer.



Some failed attempts:

* Using Uthana for animations: These all turned out wacky and worse than what Claude was doing by itself
* Upscaling services to go from my 15k tri models to cinematic-ready models: Lots of tearing, and the marginal quality increase wasn’t worth the time I’d have to spend fixing them (still have problems to fix in the existing models, don’t need to spend extra time on 1-time/rarely-used models!)
* Having Claude do some audio processing: It seemed fine with things like reverb, but when it came to pitch shifting it ended up creating very artifact-heavy music/sounds
* Getting exact compositions. I would feed Claude an image of \_exactly\_ the shot composition I wanted, and it just couldn’t get it right a lot of the time even after multiple iterations. I ended up having to compromise a lot, or have it open Blender scenes so I could manually move around the rig handles and camera. 



Where most of the time went:

* Small animation tweaks. Most of the animations were over the top and I had to make things more subtle. Also, it kept absolutely mangling hands (twisting them and creating stretching on the wrists). Some of that is still in the video, I just gave up on some scenes and even shifted the camera angles or the model rotations to hide some bs. 
* Iterating each scene to get small details right that otherwise would have been easy without AI (like feet in the ground, characters passing through walls, etc), but I really wanted to do as much as possible with AI to explore its limitations
* Claude wasting time without it showing me first: It set up endless debug scripts to try and code its sight (I didn’t let it capture my screen, because I’m a masochist and wary), and it more often than not just completely got things wrong. So I ended up going back and forth on screenshots and tiny clips to help it along so it could get a real human eye input. 



Was the output better than what I could do by myself in a weekend? **100%**

Would I do it again? **Absolutely.** 

Did I compromise on quality? **Yeah, a little. But I don’t think that the compromise was enough to offset the gains of the speed, at least not for this specific type of content.** 



I think the trailer serves its purpose (a funny quirky release trailer to get some awareness about the game), and doing it manually at this point would be an exercise of diminishing returns. 

It’s truly crazy what we can do with AI today, and I pity the “purists” that are shying away from it, because they are going to have a really hard time keeping up with everyone else.

comments.author: Kano-DracaiOfAether
comments.body: Trailer very much gave me old school red vs. blue vibes and had me laughing. Very well done. I’ll give it a look for sure. Well done!

replies.body:
Thanks!

And yes! Red vs. Blue is exactly what I meant by "old-tf2-video" vibes. I guess it was halo and my crappy memory strikes again 😅
